messages.author: 6a3b777d6a18967b
messages.subject: Auto versioning packages
parts:
The DESCRIPTION file in an R project has a Version field in it.  There seems something a bit incongruous about having that field manually set, though, and having my repo publically available on github.  Arguably every commit should increase the version number since the state of the repository has changed.  My project is fairly new and many days I've had several checkins a day.  One of the primary purposes of version numbers is so that when I get a bug report I can sync to that version to see if I can reproduce the error.  Is there any way to have that number auto increment?  

During the advanced r workshop Hadley recommended following the versioning system described in the semantic versioning website.  Has anyone experimented with writing a git hook to autoincrement that number (perhaps with a prompt asking questions which would indicate whether the major/minor/patch version should be increased)?

messages.author: b756a7daa2c2aa6d
messages.subject: Re: Auto versioning packages
parts:
Hi Ari,

I don't think need to update the version number of your package every
time you make a change. The problem is that install_github currently
captures the sha of the exact revision you installed (and saves it in
the DESCRIPTION), but we don't have any tools to surface that detail.
We'll probably add a version of sessionInfo() that also prints that,
which means you only need to increment the version number if you make
an API breaking change.

Hadley

messages.author: d34d025a513c07fc
messages.subject: Re: Auto versioning packages
parts:
On Tue, Dec 24, 2013 at 1:59 PM, <arila...@gmail.com> wrote:
> On Mon, Dec 23, 2013 at 2:42 PM, Winston Chang <winsto...@gmail.com>
> wrote:
>>
>> One of the problems with incrementing the version number with each
>> commit is that it doesn't work very well with git's distributed model.
>> If all your development is done by a single person on a single branch,
>> then auto-incrementing the version number could work. But if you have
>> multiple people working on a project, then you'll get a lot of merge
>> conflicts with the version number. And if you use branch for
>> development, even by a single person, you'll also get merge conflicts.
>>
>> With the current version of devtools, if someone installs a package
>> with install_github(), it automatically inserts information about the
>> commit and repo into the package description. For example, I've
>> installed shiny from github, and here's what's added:
>> > packageDescription('shiny')
>> [... other stuff trimmed ...]
>> GithubRepo: shiny
>> GithubUsername: rstudio
>> GithubRef: master
>> GithubSHA1: 4e0a61bd9bc94330f8aa1671bf3377bc3b854d1a
>>
>> So you can ask users to provide the hash of the commit when reporting
>> bugs.
>>
>> install() doesn't yet record the commit, but hopefully at some point
>> that will be implemented, so those who clone the repo and install
>> locally will have the SHA.
>>
>> -Winston
>
> Thanks Winston. That commit hash field will be helpful for me.
>
> I think that I'm struggling to understand how a submission to CRAN should
> relate to what's on github. Since I have travis-ci integration on github,
> it's arguable that CRAN is irrelevant, since R CMD check and my unit tests
> verify that my latest commit is good. Can you speak to what advantages
> submitting to CRAN has? I should say that I just made my first submit 5
> minutes ago.
>
> I'm also unclear about whether the project's homepage on github should
> reflect exactly what's on github or my current development. After talking
> with some coworkers I think that the best thing is if the master branch
> reflects CRAN, and I create a new branch called development that has my
> intermediary work.
>
> To be honest, I get confused when I see some projects on github that are
> also on cran, because I can't tell which version should be considered
> authoritative. One thing that's clear is that the CRAN version can never be
> ahead of the github version. But other than that I'm not sure.
>
> Ari


Oops, I forgot to hit reply-all in my previous message, so I've copied
and pasted the messages above.

The CRAN version of a package is an official release. CRAN has been
around for longer than Github or even git. Sites like Github,
Bitbucket, and R-forge are places where put their in-development code
for packages, but there's no requirement that developers use these
sites.

During development, you might have a changing API, or some
functionality might be broken or partially implemented. Even if you
have unit tests, they may not all pass, or you may have incomplete
coverage. In my experience, the development phase of a project can
often be a churning mess, and only toward the end of a release will
all the little issues get straightened out. For most end users, it's
simpler to just know they need version 0.9 of a project.

You could use the master branch so that it only contains release
versions of your project, but that would be an unusual way to go about
it. A much more common practice with git is to use tags to mark a
particular commit as "v0.9", or something like that.

Hope this helps!
-Winston
